title: The Monk Who Invented Movable Type
event_summary: In 1377, Buddhist monks at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju printed the Jikji — a collection of Zen Buddhist teachings — using movable metal type, making it the oldest known book printed with this technology, predating Gutenberg's Bible by 78 years. The monk Baegun compiled the text, and his disciples Seok Chan and Daldam oversaw its production using individually cast bronze characters arranged into pages. The technique had been developing in Korea since at least the 1230s under the Goryeo dynasty, driven by a desire to mass-produce Buddhist scriptures during the Mongol invasions.
why_forgotten: Gutenberg's press became synonymous with the printing revolution because it triggered an immediate, explosive transformation of European society, while Korean movable type remained largely confined to elite court and monastic use due to the complexity of Chinese characters and state control over printing. The Jikji itself was scattered — the only surviving copy ended up in France's Bibliothèque nationale after a French diplomat acquired it during the colonial era, and Korea's turbulent history of invasions buried its significance. Western-centric narratives of innovation consistently credited Europe as the birthplace of print culture.
why_it_matters: The Korean innovation demonstrates that the foundational technology behind the information revolution — movable type — originated in East Asia, reshaping how we understand the global history of knowledge dissemination. The Jikji was recognized by UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001, forcing a reassessment of Eurocentric technological timelines. It also reveals how political and social context, not just invention, determines whether a technology transforms civilization — the same idea that merely refined monastic practice in Korea would demolish feudal hierarchies in Europe.
